newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian govt in foreign exchange gamble - opposition.
newsitem.headline: Belgian govt in foreign exchange gamble - opposition.

text.p: Belgium's main opposition party said on Wednesday a potential loss on currency swaps taken out by a previous government was looming large over the current government's efforts to cut the state's bulging debts.
Herman de Croo, chairman of the Flemish VLD liberals, angrily told parliament that the 1989-1992 government led by Wilfried Martens had secretly speculated on the foreign exchange market.

Positions built up so far now threatened a loss to the government of 44 billion Belgian francs ($1.40 billion). De Croo said he had found out about the transactions in letters from the Court of Accounts, the state auditing body.
The deals involve strong currencies with relatively low interest rates, such as the mark, being used to buy weak ones with higher rates to boost interest income.
The transactions turn sour if the weak currencies weaken further, raising the buy-back costs in the original currency and resulting in a loss on the so-called swap.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told parliament in reply to the charge that the technique had been used, but "in no way was there any speculation against the franc".
He noted swaps would have no impact on the budget but could affect state debt.
Dehaene accused De Croo of having quoted selectively from the letters from the Court of Accounts.

De Croo's allegation came at an awkward time for Dehaene who was in parliament to defend the 1997 budget which centres on cutting the budget deficit and state debt in time for the 1999 start of Europe's single currency.
A 44 billion setback would dampen Dehaene's efforts to bring Belgium's debt-to-GDP ratio -- the highest in Europe -- down to 127.0 percent in 1997 from 130.4 percent in 1996.

Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told the Belgian news agency Belga from Washington, where he is attending the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund, that it was premature to speak of a loss on the transactions.
He said that if under today's market conditions all current transactions, due between 1997 and 2002, were exercised early the net result would be a loss of 34 billion francs.
"The Treasury has no plans to terminate these positions, so it is premature to talk about a loss."

He noted that as a result of current policy the foreign exchange share of total state debt would fall to just eight percent at the end of this year. In nominal Belgian francs terms the foreign currency debt would go down to 969 billion francs this year from 1,520 billion in 1993. ($1=31.38 Belgian Franc)
